mainTopic: Can a חרש or אלם communicate through writing or signs for a גט, for עדות and for other matters?
overview: This amud begins with the closing words of an earlier discussion: בית דין tests a mute man with questions about produce. רב כהנא then rules in the name of רב that a חרש who can express himself in writing may have a גט written for his wife. רבי זירא explains why this teaches something new. The משנה dealt only with an אלם, who can hear, while a ברייתא defines a חרש as someone who cannot hear. The גמרא then proves these definitions from a פסוק and from a common saying. Next comes a challenge from the rule that a mute cannot testify even though he can write. אביי answers that עדות is different, because it must come מפיהם ולא מפי כתבם. A ברייתא that lists testimonies, inheritances and business deals is then explained item by item so that it fits this rule. Another ברייתא says a חרש's writing does not work for גיטין. The גמרא answers that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל limits that rule to one born a חרש, and it explains the rule as being about his יבמה. It ends by asking whether the חכמים really make a גזירה about a חרש because of a פיקח, and that question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Closing the previous discussion: testing with produce
steps.stepSummary: The previous discussion about how בית דין tests a mute man ends: they question him about produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, they test him with questions about produce.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the closing words of the earlier discussion about how בית דין checks that a mute man is mentally clear. The גמרא settles that the test questions are about פירות (produce).
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אלא shows that an earlier suggestion was turned down and is now replaced. The final answer is that the testing questions concern produce. Questions like these show whether the man's mind is clear.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; it introduces a replacement for an idea that was rejected

phrases.english: Rather, with produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the discussion that came just before this section on the daf.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacement answer: the test is done with questions about produce.
steps.terutzMaskana: בית דין tests the mute man's clarity with questions about produce.

steps.title: A deaf man who can write may divorce his wife
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא, in the name of רב, rules that a חרש who expresses himself in writing may have a גט written and given for his wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said in the name of רב: if a חרש can express himself through writing, we write a גט and give it to his wife.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא reports a ruling from רב. A חרש who can communicate by writing can divorce his wife through his written instructions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חרש is usually treated as lacking legal competence. רב says that clear writing shows his mind is working, so his written instructions are enough for a גט. This ruling is the base that the rest of this section discusses.

keyTerms.meaning: A deaf person (in this case, one who also cannot speak)

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up the whole question of whether writing can show the legal competence of someone who cannot hear.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said that Rav said:
A deaf person who can speak through writing,
we write and give a bill of divorce to his wife.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A חרש who can express himself in writing may divorce his wife based on his written instructions.

steps.title: What is new here? The משנה already taught this
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף challenges רב: the משנה already said that a man who became mute can give a גט after he is tested.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: what is he teaching us? We already learned in the משנה: a man became mute, and they asked him, 'Shall we write a גט for your wife?' and he nodded. They test him three times. If he answers 'no' to questions whose answer is no and 'yes' to questions whose answer is yes, they write the גט and give it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף asks why רב needed to say this at all. The משנה already teaches that someone who cannot speak but communicates clearly can give a גט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is that רב's ruling seems to add nothing. If a nod from a mute man is enough after testing, written instructions should obviously be enough too. רב יוסף assumes the man in the משנה and the man in רב's ruling are the same kind of case.

keyTerms.meaning: What is he teaching us? (Isn't this already known?)

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
What is he teaching us?
We learned: If he became mute,
and they said to him: "Shall we write a bill of divorce for your wife?"
and he nodded his head,
they test him three times;
if to a 'no' question he said "no,"
and to a 'yes' question, "yes,"
then these may write and give it.
phrases.notes: "These" are the people the husband asked to arrange the גט.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's ruling in step 2 as unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling about a חרש who writes.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה already allows a man who cannot speak to give a גט based on signs, so the ruling seems to teach nothing new.

steps.title: An אלם is different from a חרש
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא answers that the משנה deals with an אלם, who can hear and is fully competent. רב's case is a חרש, which is a new teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said to him: are you talking about a mute? A mute is different. As a ברייתא teaches: one who speaks but cannot hear is a חרש; one who hears but cannot speak is an אלם; and both are like competent people in all their matters.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא defends רב. The משנה only taught about an אלם, a man who can still hear, while רב was talking about someone who cannot hear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אלם can hear, so he counts as fully competent, and his nod is easy to accept. רב's ruling is about someone who can neither hear nor speak, who would normally be treated as not competent. רב teaches that clear writing is enough to show that this person's mind is sound, and that is new.

keyTerms.meaning: A mute, one who hears but cannot speak

steps.confusionAlert: In most places, the word חרש means someone who can neither hear nor speak, and such a person is treated as not legally competent. This ברייתא uses חרש for someone who only cannot hear, and it says he IS competent. Do not mix up the two uses of the word.
steps.whatToRemember: An אלם (hears but cannot speak) is clearly competent. רב's חידוש is about someone who cannot hear: his writing proves he is competent.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said to him:
You are talking about a mute?
A mute is different,

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: מְדַבֵּר וְאֵינוֹ שׁוֹמֵעַ – זֶהוּ חֵרֵשׁ,
phrases.english: as it is taught: one who speaks but does not hear, this is a deaf person;
one who hears but does not speak, this is a mute;
and this one and that one are like competent people
in all their matters.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יוסף's challenge from step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: the man in the משנה is a different kind of case from the man in רב's ruling.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב יוסף thought the mute man in the משנה was the same case as רב's חרש.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about an אלם, who can hear and is clearly competent. רב adds that even someone who cannot hear or speak can give a גט through writing.

steps.title: Where do these definitions come from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that a חרש is one who cannot hear and an אלם is one who cannot speak.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how do we know that one who speaks but does not hear is a חרש, and one who hears but does not speak is an אלם?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how we know the definitions the ברייתא used. It is setting up the next step, which will bring the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer to רב יוסף depends completely on these definitions. So the גמרא wants a source showing that the word חרש is about hearing and the word אלם is about speaking.

phrases.aramaic: וּמִמַּאי דִּמְדַבֵּר וְאֵינוֹ שׁוֹמֵעַ זֶהוּ חֵרֵשׁ,
phrases.english: And from where do we know that one who speaks but does not hear is a deaf person,
and one who hears but does not speak is a mute?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the definitions in the ברייתא from step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source for defining חרש as someone who cannot hear and אלם as someone who cannot speak.

steps.title: Proof from a פסוק in תהלים
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק links חרש with not hearing and אלם with not opening one's mouth.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And I am like a חרש, I do not hear, and like an אלם who does not open his mouth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק. It pairs חרש with not hearing and אלם with not speaking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק itself explains each word: the חרש does not hear, and the אלם does not open his mouth. This supports the ברייתא's definitions.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (in a פסוק)
He will not open his mouth

phrases.english: As it is written:
"And I am like a deaf man, I do not hear,
and like a mute who does not open his mouth."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק in תהלים 38:14 connects חרש with not hearing and אלם with not speaking.

steps.title: Second answer: what people say
steps.stepSummary: Another source: common speech, which calls a mute someone whose 'speech has been taken away.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say it is like people say: 'his speech has been taken away.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to know what אלם means. It points to an everyday Aramaic expression.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People describe an אלם as someone whose speech was taken away. This shows that the word is about losing speech, not hearing. Language people really use can help define a word.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces another answer)
His speech has been taken away

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
as people say:
"His speech has been taken away."
phrases.notes: This is a play on sounds. The word אלם is read as a short form of this phrase about losing one's speech.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to step 5, in addition to the פסוק in step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Everyday speech describes an אלם as someone whose speech was taken away, so אלם means someone who cannot speak.

steps.title: רבי זירא's real difficulty: a mute is exempt from testifying even though he can write
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא says his real difficulty with רב comes from a ברייתא. The ברייתא exempts an אלם from testifying because he 'cannot tell,' even though he could tell through writing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: If anything bothers me, this is what bothers me. A ברייתא says: 'If he does not tell' excludes a mute, who cannot tell. But why? He can tell through writing!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא brings a ברייתא that seems to show writing does not count as 'telling.' That would be a problem for רב, who lets a חרש give a גט through writing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק punishes a witness who does not testify, and the ברייתא says a mute is excluded because he cannot tell. But a mute can write. If writing counted, he should not be excluded. So it looks like writing is not a valid way to communicate, and that goes against רב.

keyTerms.term: אִי קַשְׁיָא לִי – הָא קַשְׁיָא לִי
keyTerms.meaning: If anything is difficult for me, this is what is difficult for me

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:

phrases.aramaic: אִי קַשְׁיָא לִי – הָא קַשְׁיָא לִי,
phrases.english: If anything is difficult for me, this is what is difficult for me,
phrases.notes: He means: if I have a problem with רב's ruling about writing, here is the real problem.

phrases.english: as it is taught in a ברייתא: "If he does not tell"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:1. This is about a witness who refuses to testify.

phrases.english: this excludes a mute, who is not able to tell.

phrases.aramaic: אַמַּאי? הָא יָכוֹל לְהַגִּיד מִתּוֹךְ הַכְּתָב!
phrases.english: Why? He is able to tell through writing!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי קַשְׁיָא לִי – הָא קַשְׁיָא לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge to רב's ruling after the definitions of חרש and אלם were settled.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that a חרש who can communicate through writing may give a גט.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא excludes an אלם from testifying even though he can write. So writing must not count as valid communication.

steps.title: אביי: testimony is different because it must come from the mouth
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that עדות has a special rule. The Torah requires testimony from the witnesses' mouths, not from their writing.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: You are bringing a proof from testimony? Testimony is different, because the Torah says 'from their mouths,' and not from their writing.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי defends רב. He says the ברייתא about the mute only shows something about עדות, which has its own special rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Writing can be valid communication in general. עדות is an exception, because the Torah demands spoken testimony. So the mute's exemption from testifying tells us nothing about a גט.

keyTerms.meaning: From their mouths and not from their writing

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a well-known rule: עדות must be given orally and not in writing.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
You are speaking about testimony?
Testimony is different,
because the Merciful One said: "From their mouths"
phrases.notes: This comes from the פסוק 'על פי שנים עדים' (דברים 17:6), which is read as 'from their own mouths.'

phrases.english: and not from their writing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: עֵדוּת קָאָמְרַתְּ? שָׁאנֵי עֵדוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי זירא's difficulty by limiting it to עדות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: עדות has a special rule from a פסוק that does not apply elsewhere.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The mute's exemption from testifying shows that writing is never valid communication.
steps.terutzMaskana: Writing can work in general. Only עדות requires speech, because of מפיהם ולא מפי כתבם.

steps.title: Challenge: a ברייתא says a mute is tested for testimonies too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אביי from a ברייתא. It says a man who lost his speech is tested for עדיות, just like for גיטין, so it seems he can testify.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: Just as they test him for divorce documents, so too they test him for business deals, gifts, testimonies, and inheritances. In any event it says 'testimonies'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks אביי's answer with a ברייתא that puts testimony on the same list as divorce documents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a mute person can be tested and then give עדות, then עדות is not limited to speech. That contradicts אביי's claim that testimony must come only 'from their mouths.'

keyTerms.meaning: They test him (to check his understanding)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
Just as they test him for divorce documents,
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the man from the משנה who lost his ability to speak.

phrases.english: so too they test him for business deals and for gifts,
for testimonies, and for inheritances.
In any event, it teaches "testimonies"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's answer that עדות requires speech.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's rule that עדות must be מפיהם ולא מפי כתבם.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא lists עדיות among the things a mute person can be tested for. That implies he can testify without speech.

steps.title: רב ששת: that ברייתא means testimony for a woman, where the רבנן were lenient
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the ברייתא's 'testimonies' means עדות אשה, testimony that a woman's husband died. There the רבנן were lenient.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף בר מניומי said that רב ששת said: The ברייתא is talking about testimony for a woman, where the רבנן were lenient.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת defends אביי's rule. He limits the ברייתא to one special kind of testimony.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In general, עדות must be spoken. But to let a woman whose husband died remarry, the רבנן accepted testimony that normally would not count. That is why a mute's testimony can work in that case.

keyTerms.meaning: Testimony that lets a woman remarry (that her husband died)

steps.whatToRemember: In general, עדות must be spoken: מפיהם ולא מפי כתבם. The exception is עדות אשה, where the רבנן were lenient, so even a mute person who is tested may testify.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't conclude that written or mute testimony is valid in general. The ברייתא's 'testimonies' refers only to the lenient case of a woman whose husband died.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi said that Rav Sheshet said:
This is about testimony for a woman,
phrases.notes: Testimony that her husband died, so she is allowed to remarry.

phrases.english: where the Rabbis were lenient with her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: בְּעֵדוּת אִשָּׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the ברייתא by limiting 'testimonies' to עדות אשה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the ברייתא to a special case where the רבנן were lenient.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא shows that a mute person can give any kind of testimony.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only in עדות אשה is a mute person's testimony accepted. Ordinary עדות still must be spoken.

steps.title: But the ברייתא also lists inheritances
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב ששת: the same ברייתא also lists 'inheritances,' which is a money matter, not עדות אשה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the ברייתא also teaches 'inheritances'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב ששת's answer by pointing to another word in the same ברייתא: 'inheritances.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת said the mute is only accepted for עדות אשה, where the רבנן were lenient. But the ברייתא also says he is tested for 'inheritances.' That sounds like testimony about money, where full proper testimony is needed. So it seems a mute can testify after all.

keyTerms.meaning: But it teaches! (a challenge from the wording of a source)

phrases.english: But it teaches: 'Inheritances'!
phrases.notes: This is another item in the same ברייתא from Step 10, about the man who lost his speech.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב ששת's answer in Step 11 using another word in the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's claim that the ברייתא only accepts the mute for עדות אשה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Inheritances' is a money matter, not עדות אשה. So the ברייתא seems to accept the mute's testimony in a regular case.

steps.title: It means the inheritance of his own firstborn
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו explains that 'inheritances' means the man saying which of his own sons is the בכור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: It means the inheritance of his firstborn son.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו answers the challenge. The 'inheritances' in the ברייתא are about the man's own family, not testimony about other people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man is not testifying about someone else's money. He is identifying which of his sons is the בכור, who gets a double share. That is like dividing up his own property, so it does not need formal testimony.

keyTerms.meaning: His firstborn son, who gets a double share

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said:
The inheritance of his firstborn son.
phrases.notes: He means the father points out which son is his בכור. He is dealing with his own property, not judging other people's.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: 'inheritances' refers only to the man's own firstborn
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Inheritances' meant regular testimony about other people's money.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means identifying his own בכור, which is not formal testimony.

steps.title: But it also lists business and gifts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: the ברייתא lists 'business and gifts.' Doesn't that mean he testifies about these for other people?
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case it teaches 'for business and for gifts.' What, doesn't that mean for everyone else?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more challenge from the same ברייתא, this time from the words 'business and gifts.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if 'inheritances' is explained away, the ברייתא also says he is tested for business deals and gifts. That sounds like he may testify about other people's deals. If so, a mute can testify.

keyTerms.meaning: For everyone else, for other people

phrases.english: In any case, it teaches:
'For business and for gifts,'
What, is it not for everyone else?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After 'inheritances' was explained, the גמרא challenges from a different phrase in the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of אביי and רב ששת that a mute cannot give regular testimony
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'business and gifts' means testifying about other people's deals, then a mute's testimony is accepted in money matters.

steps.title: No, it means his own deals
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'business and gifts' means the mute's own transactions, not testimony for others.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, for himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers briefly: the business and gifts are the mute's own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא means that before a mute buys, sells or gives a gift, the court checks that his mind is clear. This is about his own actions, not about testifying for others. So the rule that עדות must come 'from their mouths' still stands.
steps.whatToRemember: Every item in the ברייתא about the man who lost his speech is explained as either עדות אשה, where the רבנן were lenient, or the man's own affairs. None of them is regular testimony about others, so אביי's rule stays in place.

phrases.english: No, for himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: his own transactions only
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Business and gifts' meant testifying about other people's deals.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means the mute's own deals, which the court checks him for.

steps.title: A ברייתא says a חרש's writing does not work for גיטין
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב כהנא from a ברייתא: a חרש's signs and writing are followed only for movable property, not for גיטין.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא raises an objection: With a deaf-mute, we follow his hand signals, his lip movements and his handwriting only for movable property, but not for bills of divorce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא to attack רב כהנא's earlier ruling that a חרש who can write may have a גט written and given to his wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says a חרש may communicate by signs or writing, but only for movable property. It says clearly: 'not for גיטין.' That seems to go directly against רב כהנא's ruling that his writing is enough for a גט.

phrases.english: They raised an objection: A deaf-mute,
they did not follow his signals
and his lip movements and his handwriting,
phrases.notes: קְפִיצוֹתָיו literally means 'his jumpings.' Here it means the movements of his lips.

phrases.english: except for movable property;
but not for bills of divorce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of testimony and goes back to challenge the main ruling about a חרש who writes a גט.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב כהנא's ruling that a חרש who can write may have a גט written and given to his wife
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא openly says a חרש's handwriting does not work for גיטין.

steps.title: A dispute between תנאים: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this is a dispute between תנאים. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the ban is only for someone born a חרש. Someone who could hear and later became a חרש can write the instruction for his גט, and the witnesses sign.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a dispute between תנאים, as it is taught: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said: When is this said? With someone who was a deaf-mute from the start. But a competent person who later became a deaf-mute writes, and they sign.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב כהנא's ruling follows a different תנא, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who limits the ban.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא in Step 16 is one opinion. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the ban on גיטין is only for someone who was a חרש from birth. A person who once had full abilities and later became a חרש can write the instruction, and the witnesses sign the גט. רב כהנא follows this view.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a dispute between תנאים
In what case was this said? (limits a rule)
A fully capable person, who can hear and speak

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, it matters when the person became a חרש. Someone born that way cannot give a גט through writing. Someone who became a חרש later can write the instruction, and the witnesses sign. רב כהנא's ruling fits this view.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא does not reject the ברייתא of Step 16. It says that ברייתא is one side of a dispute between תנאים, and רב כהנא follows the other side.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a common way the גמרא defends an אמורא: when a ברייתא contradicts him, it shows another תנא who agrees with him.

phrases.english: It is a dispute between Tannaim –

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, אָמַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל:
phrases.english: as it is taught, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said:
In what case is this said?
With one who was a deaf-mute from the start,
but a competent person who became a deaf-mute –
he writes and they sign.
phrases.notes: 'He writes' the instruction to give the גט; 'they' are the witnesses, who sign the גט.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 16 by showing a תנא who disagrees with that ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Dispute between תנאים: the ruling follows a different תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא banning a חרש's writing for גיטין is the only opinion, so רב כהנא is contradicted.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל limits the ban to one born a חרש, and רב כהנא follows him.

steps.title: Why can't a born deaf-mute divorce with signs?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ruling that a חרש מעיקרו cannot divorce with signs. He married her with signs, so he should be able to divorce her with signs.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a man who was a deaf-mute from birth cannot? Just as he marries her through signs, so too he should send her away through signs!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the ruling from step 17 that a man born a חרש cannot give a גט using signs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A born חרש can only marry through signs (רמיזה), and that marriage is valid only by rabbinic law. Something made through signs should be undone through signs. So why does the ruling stop him from divorcing that way?

keyTerms.meaning: Hinting, communicating by gestures or signs
He marries her (literally, brings her in)
He divorces her (literally, sends her out)

phrases.english: And one who was a deaf-mute from the start — cannot?!
phrases.notes: This is a surprised question about רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's rule from step 17.

phrases.english: Just as he marries her through signs,
so too he divorces her through signs!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction drawn in step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a חרש מעיקרו cannot write a גט
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Symmetry: a marriage made through signs should be undone through signs.

steps.title: The case is about his יבמה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא agrees that with his own wife he could divorce through signs. The ruling is talking about a יבמה he married through ייבום.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is about his wife, that is indeed so. What are we dealing with here? With his יבמה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא agrees with the challenge for an ordinary wife. Then it says the ruling is really about a יבמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wife he married through signs can be divorced through signs. A יבמה is different, because her bond to him can come from Torah law. Signs are not strong enough to undo a Torah-level bond.

keyTerms.meaning: Indeed, so it is (agreeing with the question)
What case are we dealing with here?
His brother's widow, who falls to him for ייבום

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying a born חרש can never divorce. With his own wife he can use signs. Only the יבמה case is limited.

phrases.english: If it is about his wife, indeed so;
phrases.notes: He means a wife he married himself through signs.

phrases.english: here, what are we dealing with —
with his יבמה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 18 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ruling is about any wife of a born חרש.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ruling is only about his יבמה, whose bond is stronger than his signs.

steps.title: Which brother did the יבמה come from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which brother the יבמה came from. If he was a חרש, her marriage to him was only through signs, so she could still be divorced with signs.
steps.simpleTranslation: His יבמה from whom? If you say she fell to him from his deaf-mute brother, then just as her marriage was through signs, so too her divorce can be through signs!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks the new answer by asking which brother died and left her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the dead brother was also a חרש, he married her only through signs. Her tie to the יבם then comes from a rabbinic-level marriage. So signs should be enough to end it, and the challenge from step 18 returns.

keyTerms.meaning: She fell to him (became bound to him for ייבום)

phrases.english: His יבמה — from whom?
If you say she fell to him from his deaf-mute brother —
just as her marriage was through signs,
phrases.notes: This means her first marriage, to the brother who was a חרש.

phrases.english: so too her divorce is through signs!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the יבמה answer of step 19.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the dead brother was a חרש, the bond is only rabbinic, so signs should be enough to end it.

steps.title: She came from a hearing brother
steps.stepSummary: The case is a יבמה who came from a פיקח brother. Her bond is from the Torah, so signs cannot end it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, she fell to him from his competent brother.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the dead brother was a פיקח, a fully competent person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פיקח brother's marriage was a full Torah marriage, so the bond of ייבום is from the Torah too. The חרש's signs work only by rabbinic law, so they cannot cancel it.

keyTerms.meaning: A fully competent person who can hear and speak

phrases.english: Rather, she fell to him from his competent brother.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 20 by picking the other option.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The יבמה might have come from a חרש brother.
steps.terutzMaskana: She came from a פיקח brother, so her bond is Torah-level and signs cannot end it.

steps.title: A decree because of the hearing brother
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: even if she came from a חרש brother, the חכמים made a גזירה so people won't confuse it with the case of a פיקח brother.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you wish, say: actually she fell to him from his deaf-mute brother, and there is a decree on the deaf-mute brother's case because of the competent brother's case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way to answer step 20. It keeps the case of a חרש brother and explains the ban as a rabbinic decree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By strict law, signs would be enough when the brother was a חרש. But people might not tell the two cases apart. So the חכמים banned divorce by signs here too, to protect the case of a פיקח brother.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces another answer)
A rabbinic decree made to prevent a mistake

steps.whatToRemember: A born חרש can divorce his own wife with signs. He cannot divorce his יבמה that way: either her bond is from the Torah (a פיקח brother), or there is a גזירה (a חרש brother).

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
actually, she fell to him from his deaf-mute brother,

phrases.aramaic: וּגְזֵירָה אָחִיו חֵרֵשׁ אַטּוּ אָחִיו פִּיקֵּחַ.
phrases.english: and it is a decree: the deaf-mute brother's case because of the competent brother's case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to step 20, different from step 21.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With a חרש brother, signs should be enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: The חכמים banned signs there too, because of the case of a פיקח brother.

steps.title: Then his own wife should be included too
steps.stepSummary: If the חכמים made a גזירה for a יבמה from a חרש brother, they should also make one for the חרש's own wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then his wife too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the second answer. If the חכמים worry about confusion, they should also stop a חרש from divorcing his own wife with signs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 22 said the חכמים blocked divorce by signs for a יבמה from a חרש brother so people would not mix her up with a יבמה from a פיקח brother. The גמרא asks: by that logic, why not also block it for his own wife? Back in Step 19 we agreed he can divorce his own wife with signs.

keyTerms.meaning: If so. Used to show a problem that follows from what was just said.
His wife. Here, the woman the חרש married himself through signs.

phrases.english: If so,
phrases.notes: He means: if the חכמים really made a גזירה out of fear of confusion, as Step 22 said.

phrases.english: his wife too!
phrases.notes: He means that the חכמים should also stop a חרש from divorcing his own wife with signs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reach of the גזירה proposed in Step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: The second answer (Step 22), that the חכמים made a גזירה for a יבמה from a חרש brother.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If fear of confusion is enough to make a גזירה, the same fear should also stop divorce by signs for the חרש's own wife. That would go against Step 19.

steps.title: A יבמה gets confused with a יבמה, but a wife does not
steps.stepSummary: People might mix up one יבמה with another, but nobody would mix up a man's own wife with a יבמה, so no גזירה was needed for his wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: His יבמה can be confused with his other יבמה, but his wife cannot be confused with his יבמה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. A גזירה is only needed where real confusion is likely, and that only happens between two kinds of יבמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A יבמה from a חרש brother and a יבמה from a פיקח brother look like the same kind of case, since both came through ייבום. So people could mix them up. A wife he married himself is a completely different kind of case from a יבמה, so no one would confuse them, and no גזירה was made for her.

keyTerms.meaning: His יבמה, the widow of his brother whom he married through ייבום

steps.whatToRemember: The חכמים make a גזירה only where there is a real chance of confusion. Two kinds of יבמה can be confused with each other, but a wife and a יבמה cannot.

phrases.english: His יבמה is confused with his יבמה,
phrases.notes: The first יבמה is the one from his חרש brother. The second is a יבמה from his פיקח brother.

phrases.english: his wife is not confused with his יבמה.

steps.triggerLanguage: יְבִמְתּוֹ בִּיבִמְתּוֹ מִיחַלְּפָא, אִשְׁתּוֹ בִּיבִמְתּוֹ לָא מִיחַלְּפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: confusion is only likely between two cases of the same kind.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Fear of confusion should stretch to every case of divorce by signs, including his own wife.
steps.terutzMaskana: The גזירה covers only a יבמה from a חרש brother, because only she could be confused with a יבמה from a פיקח brother. His own wife is a different kind of case.

steps.title: Do we make a גזירה for a חרש because of a פיקח?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the whole idea of Step 22: is it really our practice to make a גזירה about a חרש because of a case involving a פיקח?
steps.simpleTranslation: And do we make a גזירה for a חרש because of a פיקח?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge against the second answer itself. This sets up the next move, and the answer comes in the next part of the daf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 22 said the חכמים made a גזירה for a יבמה from a חרש brother because of a יבמה from a פיקח brother. The גמרא now asks whether that kind of גזירה really exists. A חרש and a פיקח are very different, so maybe the חכמים would not make one because of the other.

keyTerms.meaning: We make a גזירה, a rabbinic protective decree
Because of, out of concern for
A person who can hear and speak and is fully competent

phrases.english: And do we make a גזירה for a חרש because of a פיקח?!
phrases.notes: He means the case of a יבמה from a חרש brother being restricted because of a יבמה from a פיקח brother, as in Step 22.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending the scope of the גזירה, the גמרא now questions whether the גזירה is valid at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: The second answer (Step 22), that the חכמים made a גזירה for a יבמה from a חרש brother because of a יבמה from a פיקח brother.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The question suggests that a חרש and a פיקח are different enough that we do not make a גזירה for one because of the other. If so, the basis of the second answer falls away.
